text: A referendum on joining the European Union was held in Norway on 27 and 28 November 1994. After prolonged debate, the "no" side won with 52.2 per cent of the vote, achieved on a turnout of 88.6 per cent. Norway had previously rejected EU membership in a 1972 referendum and had also been blocked from joining in 1962 by a French veto. As of 2025, this remains the most recent referendum in Norway. The "No" campaign was led by Anne Enger Lahnstein, leader of the Centre Party. Key arguments of the "No" side included concerns over loss of sovereignty and fundamental differences in economic structure, as Norway's economy relies heavily on natural resources such as oil and fish, unlike the EU's more industrial economy. Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland led the "Yes" campaign; her Labour Party was divided on the issue, and unlike Trygve Bratteli in 1972, she did not threaten to resign if the referendum resulted in a "no" vote, citing the risk of deeper party divisions. The "Yes" campaign argued that Norway, as a European country, should be part of the European Union and that membership would benefit Norway's economy. According to John Erik Fossum, a political science professor at ARENA, Centre for European Studies, University of Oslo, the fact that Norway had already signed the EEA agreement made it easier for people to vote "no" because they knew Norway had secured EU market access.
